title: FROM MATHEMATICAL SUPERINTELLIGENCE TO PHYSICAL DISCOVERY
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence suggest that coordinated populations of capablereasoning agents may solve mathematical problems of extraordinary complexity. Suchachievements raise a distinct question: Can comparable systems advance fundamental physicsby identifying the physical mechanisms responsible for nature’s observed behavior, rather thanmerely extending mathematical descriptions already accepted by scientific convention?This paper proposes a human-directed, observation-first AI research architecture forinvestigating Space-Phase (SP3) theory. SP3 proposes that physical space is a participatingmedium interacting with energy through nested configurations, conditioning, memory, andrelaxation. It seeks common explanations for matter formation, wave behavior, magnetism,gravity, galaxy dynamics, and cosmological development.A practical obstacle is the imbalance between established scientific literature, extensivelyrepresented in language-model training, and less widely circulated alternative research. Theauthor reports 1,098 SP3 papers deposited on Zenodo as of November 12, 2026. Publicavailability does not establish their inclusion in major models’ training data. This paperproposes retrieval-augmented reasoning, version-controlled mechanism registries, independentobservation auditing, and adversarial comparison with established physics. Occam’s razorSP3 Space-Phase Theory • AI-Assisted Physical Discoveryshould favor mechanisms that explain reliable observations, preserve quantitative successes,predict new outcomes, and require fewer independent assumptions. The Ship Neutron thoughtexperiment and NGC 628 study are proposed as complementary initial investigations.

title: Two Kinds of Complexity and Distributed Brakes Heterogeneous Homeostatic Loops, Same-Source Correlation and an AGI Outside Evolution
abstract: Abstract It is commonly assumed that a sufficiently intelligent agent comes with its own constraints. Evolution answers otherwise: constraints are not built into intelligence but are a second system that co-evolved with it. This paper puts that intuition into a checkable form. First, there are two kinds of complexity, neither implying the other: parametric or fitting complexity, and heterogeneous homeostatic differentiation—how many loops inside a system each have their own set point, their own reading channel, and can veto the main action on their own. Evolution grew the two roughly together; large models and AGI are the first large systems to grow along the first axis alone. Second, “the more complex, the more centralised” is imprecise: by Chapter Fourteen of the book and How Many Layers, centralisation is at least four separately adjustable quantities, the number of layers is set by the spectrum of screening lengths of environmental disturbances, conjunctive functions must be concentrated, and within-layer concentration has an interior optimum; rising complexity moves the location of the optimal concentration, while the brakes are distributed across the layers. Third (tier B), brakes aggregate by “any one can stop”, so the bound 1/ρ does not apply; the conditional miss when trouble comes depends on two correlations—between brakes, and between brakes and violations—and on shared blind spots. With demonstration parameters (violation rate 1%, ordinary miss of a single brake 10%), at same-source correlation 0.6 a single brake misses 0.65 of real violations and eight same-source brakes still miss 0.18; if the added heterologous brake is wholly independent of the violation, one same-source plus one heterologous brake falls to 0.065. But this advantage is extremely sensitive to the heterologous brake’s own correlation: a loading of only 0.10 on the violation factor brings “one same-source plus one heterologous” level with eight same-source brakes, because violations are tail events and tails amplify small correlations. The design implication must therefore be written as a conditional on both correlations, and heterology must be measured. Fourth (tier B), biological brakes are self-paid, own their readings and lie beyond the reach of the main optimiser, whereas external brakes are maintained and rewritable, are eroded one by one in order of “the delay of keeping them ÷ the cost of removing them”, and may be switched off together by one switch; intelligence itself turns self-paid brakes into maintained ones. Fifth (tier B), disagreement is the bill for brakes: the couplings that produce conflict are the couplings that produce vetoes. When each brake is calibrated separately, lowering their correlation lowers joint blindness and raises joint false alarms; when joint false alarms are calibrated to a common level, lower correlation is better on both counts, and the bill reduces to the cost of adjudicating disagreements—while joint calibration is itself a shared switch. Sixth (tier B), the cleansing paradox: using one AI to remove reading conflicts among many people raises the correlation between their readings; in the demonstration, the effective number of independent readings among a thousand people falls from about 9.9 to about 1.8. Seventh, a mechanism proxy of R-1 and R-2 has received a preliminary execution: on existing annotations of real LLM guardrails, the lift with which two models from the same developer fail together is 20.4, against a median of 4.9 across developers, in the same direction as existing large-sample studies; on controlled monitors facing disguised attacks against the primary guard, the conditional miss of same-substrate second-line monitors when the primary misses is 0.94, that of fully heterologous ones 0.34, although the latter are worse on their own—second-line brakes should be chosen by their conditional miss when the primary misses, not by stand-alone accuracy; facing topics no brake has seen, changing features or data does not help, and joint misses stay above 0.8. The disguised attacks use only four templates; robustness checks by template clusters, rotation of the primary guard and multiple seeds have their criteria fixed and remain to be run, and one deviation from the pre-registration is corrected here. From these the paper derives conditional design criteria for an external brake layer, connects them item by item to external work on homeostatic physiology, requisite variety, biological degeneracy, common-mode failure and difficulty correlation in multi-version software, conditional dependence of diagnostic tests, correlated errors of large language models, veto-player theory, the multiple hits of cancer and algorithmic monoculture, and registers five predictions testable on today’s AI systems and institutions; R-1 and R-2 have received a preliminary execution on public data in the form of a mechanism proxy, the other three have not yet been executed.

title: Automated Intracranial Aneurysm Detection and Size Extraction from Imaging Reports Using a Dual-Model Transformer Framework
abstract: Abstract Background The unstructured and variable nature of radiology reports remains a barrier to automated extraction of clinically relevant information for large-scale research and AI applications, particularly for intracranial aneurysms (IAs). Objective We aimed to develop and evaluate a dual-model transformer framework for intracranial aneurysm information extraction and assess whether structured processing improved classification and size-extraction performance compared with unstructured text. Methods We analyzed 3,183 neuroimaging reports annotated by neuroradiologists and neurosurgeons. Four encoder-based transformer models were evaluated for aneurysm-presence classification using 5-fold stratified cross-validation. A zero-shot Llama 3.1 framework was used to extract aneurysm size using direct and structured-report prompting. RadDistilBERT and Llama 3.1 were evaluated on 20 temporally distinct reports using full-report and impression-only inputs, with and without structured preprocessing. Results RadDistilBERT achieved the highest mean classification performance, with accuracy of 96.4% (± 1.8%), F1 score of 91.7% (± 10.3%), precision of 94.0% (± 4.6%), and recall of 90.7% (± 15.6%). F1 scores were 87.5% for BERT-base-uncased and 31.1% for ALBERT-base-v2. In the 20-report set, aneurysm-presence classification accuracy was 100% across all input and processing conditions. For aneurysm size extraction, structured report processing increased accuracy from 61.90% to 66.67% using the full report and from 80.95% to 85.00% using the impression section. Conclusions This study demonstrates the feasibility of a dual-model transformer framework for aneurysm-presence classification and size extraction from unstructured neuroimaging reports. RadDistilBERT achieved the strongest classification performance, while Llama 3.1 enabled zero-shot size extraction. These findings support further external validation and expansion to additional aneurysm characteristics with dedicated annotation and validation.

For aneurysm size extraction, structured report processing increased accuracy from 61.90% to 66.67% using the full report and from 80.95% to 85.00% using the impression section. Conclusions This study demonstrates the feasibility of a dual-model transformer framework for aneurysm-presence classification and size extraction from unstructured neuroimaging reports. RadDistilBERT achieved the strongest classification performance, while Llama 3.1 enabled zero-shot size extraction. These findings support further external validation and expansion to additional aneurysm characteristics with dedicated annotation and validation.

title: Intellectual Property Safeguards and the Role of Fairness in Acceptance of AI Generated Content
abstract: Abstract Public endorsement of safeguards for AI-generated creative content does not establish how strongly fairness figures in personal acceptance of that content. This cross-sectional study distinguishes these judgements using 385 adult questionnaire records from Bangladesh. We analysed four statements on creator protection, transparent balancing rules, complaint access and transparency about data and content practices, and a fifth statement on the relevance of fairness to acceptance. We estimated full response distributions, joint endorsement and paired contrasts, followed by exploratory regressions of the original fairness-salience rating. Safeguard endorsement ranged from 78.2% to 80.3%, compared with 58.4% for the salience statement. Within-person differences ranged from 19.7 to 21.8 percentage points (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Of the 301 respondents endorsing access to complaints, 176 also endorsed the salience statement. A copyright-oriented summary was associated with a higher salience rating in the adjusted model (b = 0.358, 95% CI 0.181 to 0.536; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Reported production precautions and the governance expectation summary did not meet the adjusted threshold. The association with copyright orientation persisted when the outcome was dichotomised and when the analysis was restricted to law students. The findings distinguish support for institutional protections from the reported place of fairness in personal judgement. They do not measure actual acceptance, legal compliance or the effect of changing a safeguard. The sample is concentrated in legal education and practice and does not establish national prevalence.

title: Boundary Aware Evidence Composition for Quantum Classical Compiler Debugging: An Empirical Evaluation
abstract: Quantum–classical compilation crosses represen- tation, dialect, and runtime boundaries at which different checks establish different properties. We describe producer-aware exchange, advisory inspection, compatible native verification, and artifact retention in MLIR-LLVM. An operational model links checkpoints, predicates, signature matching, localization, and costs to implementation fields and archived observations. Historical CPU measurements record a 3.770 s full-workflow median at 128 shots, with backend ordering dependent on workload and timed boundary. A remediation campaign evaluates seven faults and three controls, adds a phase-sensitive Bell witness, and executes optimized modules derived from checked inputs on a bounded CUDA-Q path. All faulty primary executions and faulty relocated replays match intended signatures, nine control executions pass. The remediation uses 299 behavioral shots per execution. Checkpoint policies reduce mean known-origin distance from 1.143 to zero, but staged and equivalent native checkpoints tie. The common executable stratum. Exploratory pipeline/check wall time is about 4.9× higher with staged checks than with final- only oracles. These observations establish selected-case detection, checkpoint localization, and same-stack repeatability.

title: Whose Readmission Gets Missed? A Fairness and Calibration Audit of Hospital Readmission Prediction
abstract: Readmission prediction models are usually reported with a single number — one AUC, computed over everyone. That number can be accurate and still hide the only question a clinician or a patient actually cares about: for whom does the model fail? We audit, rather than merely train, a 30-day readmission predictor on the UCI Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset. After first-encounter-per-patient filtering and removal of patients discharged dead or to hospice, 69,973 patients remain, of whom 9.0% were readmitted within 30 days. A gradient-boosting model reaches a test AUC of 0.636 and a logistic regression 0.624 — unremarkable, and consistent with the published ceiling for administrative readmission models. The audit is where the information is. At the software-default threshold of 0.5 the gradient-boosting model identifies zero of the 943 readmitted test patients. At a shared, validation-calibrated operating threshold, recall varies systematically: 0.41–0.82 across age bands, 0.48 for AfricanAmerican patients versus 0.65 for Caucasian patients (bootstrap confidence intervals do not overlap), and 0.58 versus 0.64 by gender — while per-group calibration error stays small everywhere (ECE ≤ 0.041). The failure is therefore not mainly miscalibration; it is the distribution of thresholded errors. We then test the standard fix, per-group thresholds fitted on validation data. It works where groups are large — the age recall gap falls from 0.404 to 0.150 and the gender gap from 0.065 to 0.016, at a cost of about one point of precision — but for race it does not close the headline gap, and in its ungated form it harms the smallest groups: the Hispanic group's recall falls from 0.556 to 0.333 because its threshold was estimated from a handful of validation positives. A support-gated variant narrows the AfricanAmerican–Caucasian gap from 0.166 to 0.099 at negligible overall cost. Our conclusion is procedural: a fairness audit that reports gaps without confidence intervals, and a mitigation applied without a minimum-support rule, can both mislead — the groups most at risk of being missed are precisely the groups too small for naive post-processing to reach.

title: MCP-MemoryBench: Validated 60-User Split with Adjudicated Gold Labels
abstract: MCP-MemoryBench tests whether a memory system for language model agents enforces supersede, delete and scope operations that are supplied to it explicitly. This record holds the data of the validated split with its adjudicated gold labels: 60 synthetic users, 629 memory items and 188 probes. It accompanies the article "Enforcing Deletion and Correction in Memory for Language Model Agents: A Benchmark and a Reference Implementation" by Arda Altınörs and Bekir Tevfik Akgün. README.md is the datasheet and describes the file formats. All users and facts are synthetic.

title: Kaa-Corpus: Karakalpak Wikipedia Monolingual Corpus (v1.1)
abstract: Kaa-Corpus is a monolingual sentence-level corpus of Karakalpak (ISO 639-3 kaa), a Kipchak Turkic language spoken mainly in the Republic of Karakalpakstan, Uzbekistan. It is written in the 2016 Karakalpak Latin alphabet. All text comes from 887 Karakalpak Wikipedia articles written by one author, Bekbosin Kalmuratov (Wikipedia user Bekan88): original articles in Karakalpak and high-quality translations of English Wikipedia articles made by the author. The articles were created between May 2023 and November 2025. Information technology accounts for 74.7% of the articles, sport for 13.4% and film/TV for 8.1%. v1.1 (cleaned, recommended), kaa_corpus_v1.1.jsonl: 61,602 records, 1,092,758 words, 89,661 unique word forms. Unicode NFC normalisation, Cyrillic homoglyph repair, removal of Wikipedia footnote markers and file captions, exact deduplication. v1.0 (original), karakalpak_corpus_v1_1M.txt: 62,983 lines, 1,098,626 words. The record also includes full documentation (README), statistics, a list of source articles with topics, reproducible Python scripts, figures, and a stratified random sample of 400 records with an expert-evaluation form. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (derived from Karakalpak Wikipedia). Also available on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/bekan/karakalpak_corpus_v1_m

title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
abstract: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.

title: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models
abstract: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to **23x** rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io

title: eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation
abstract: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student's update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student's final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student's final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student's final output distribution matches the teacher's, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.

title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
abstract: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. We compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld, and use JEV as a teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop. As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.

Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.

title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
abstract: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).

title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors
abstract: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.

title: MMAligner: Safeguarding Multimodal Large Language Models through Representation Calibration
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often refuse unsafe text prompts yet generate harmful responses to semantically equivalent multimodal inputs. Existing defenses either rely on external guardrails, which add inference overhead without repairing intrinsic flaws, or safety fine-tuning, which treats alignment as black-box optimization and may sacrifice utility or require large multimodal datasets. To identify the cause of this safety disparity, we analyze MLLM representations geometrically. We find that safety mechanisms learned from text persist across modalities: a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary remain effective, and representations inside this boundary consistently trigger refusals. However, unsafe multimodal inputs undergo a representation shift that places most of them outside the boundary, allowing them to bypass the model's intrinsic safety mechanism. This indicates that multimodal safety degradation stems from representation misalignment rather than the absence of safety capability. Based on this finding, we propose MMAligner, a safeguarding method that calibrates unsafe multimodal representations into the pre-existing refusal region. MMAligner applies a hard lower bound to ensure refusal, a soft upper bound to avoid excessive modification, and a preservation objective for benign inputs. Experiments across multiple open-source MLLMs show that MMAligner raises the average refusal rate on unsafe multimodal inputs to 99% with less than 2% utility degradation and minimal training data, substantially improving the safety-utility trade-off over existing baselines. title: ShapeUpLMD: Automated spatial optimization of laser microdissection for tissue sampling
abstract: Abstract Laser microdissection (LMD) enables enrichment of defined cellular populations from heterogeneous tissues, providing histologically-resolved molecular profiles with spatial resolution. However, the absence of standardized methods for generating optimized regions of interest (ROIs) limits reproducibility and scalability for spatial multi-omic workflows. To address this gap, we developed ShapeUpLMD, an open-source software tool and integrated workflow that automates the optimization of spatially defined ROIs for LMD, directly from digital pathology annotations. Fresh-frozen uterine serous carcinoma (USC) tumors (n = 11) were sectioned onto polyethylene naphthalate slides, scanned and subsequently annotated by an expert pathologist. Tumor and non-tumor ROIs were used to train tumor-specific classifiers in HALO (Indica Labs). Classified tumor or unbiased whole tissue ROIs were refined and optimized by ShapeUpLMD prior to automated collection on a Leica LMD7 microscope. Across the cohort, predicted tumor ROIs increased effective tumor purity by 86 ± 6% relative to whole tissue while maintaining high spatial concordance between predicted and collected ROIs (accuracy = 0.9 ± 0.05). Data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry quantified upwards of ∼6,500 proteins across spatially resolved ROIs, revealing regionally coherent clustering of adjacent tumor regions and abundance patterns consistent with tumor and non-tumor cell admixture in an unbiased spatial proteomic application. ShapeUpLMD provides an automated, reproducible, and scalable framework that bridges digital pathology with LMD enabling high-fidelity spatial enrichment for multi-omic analyses. This workflow increases throughput, reduces inter-operator variability, and supports standardized, regionally resolved tissue collection for spatial systems biology applications. The software is available at https://github.com/GYNCOE/ShapeUpLMD .

title: Back to Pixels: Lifting Latent Video Diffusion into Pixel Space
abstract: Frontier video generation models work in a VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. This compression made training tractable, but now limits high-resolution, controllable, and interactive generation -- doubling resolution quadruples token count, conditions apply to groups of frames rather than individual ones, and each response must wait for the rest of its multi-frame block. We present PixVid, a simple yet effective method that lifts a pretrained latent video model to directly generate every frame in pixel space. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with a convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within $\sim 1.3$M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at $2\times$ higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: https://chenshuo20.github.io/PixVid/

title: Identification automatique de domaines de connaissances dans un dictionnaire universel du XVIIIe s.
abstract: On se propose de présenter les résultats d’une recherche visant à l’identification et à la classification automatique de domaines de connaissances dans un dictionnaire universel du XVIIIe siècle.L’œuvre support des analyses est l’édition de 1743 du Dictionnaire Universel François & Latin (désormais, DUFLT) dit de Trévoux. Environ 20 % des articles héberge un ou plusieurs paragraphes associés à une marque de domaine (Pétrequin 2009, Turcan 2024) qui stipule de quelle science (astronomie ...), art (poësie ... forge...) ou métier (charron ...) relève le contenu. On est loin de la systématicité de l’Encyclopédie de Diderot et d’Alembert (1751-1772) où 83% environ des articles est pourvu d’une marque de domaine (données tirées de l’ARTFL et de l’ENCCRE). Notre objectif est de parvenir à une classification complète de l’ensemble des paragraphes du dictionnaire en leur affectant un ou plusieurs domaines de connaissance. Pour ce faire, nous développons une approche combinant grands modèles de langage (LLMs) et modèles de classification supervisée. On soulignera que la classification en domaines de connaissances a déjà fait l’objet de plusieurs études computationnelles sur l’Encyclopédie de Diderot & d’Alembert (Horton et al. 2009, Roe et al. 2016, Brenon et al. 2022), mais qu’aucune n’a été conduite à ce jour sur le DUFLT.Dans une première partie, nous présenterons les choix méthodologiques qui structurent notre démarche. Nous justifierons le choix du paragraphe comme unité de base de nos analyses, le regroupement des marques de domaine (simples : en termes de géographie ...; complexes : Terme de Botanique & de Pharmacie) en un nombre restreint de « macro-domaines ». Nous aborderons également les difficultés liées à l’hétérogénéité de ces marques et à la nature parfois pluri-/inter-disciplinaire de leurs contenus.Dans une seconde partie, nous décrirons le protocole expérimental mis en œuvre. À partir d’un ensemble de paragraphes initialement pourvus d’une ou plusieurs marques de domaine (que l’on aura retirées), nous sollicitons différents LLMs dans un cadre de classification few-shot afin de leur faire associer un ou plusieurs macro-domaines. Les prédictions sont ensuite évaluées par comparaison avec les annotations existantes. Cette phase permet d’identifier les configurations de prompts et les modèles les plus performants, et d’affiner progressivement les instructions fournies aux modèles. Les résultats préliminaires montrent qu’un des modèles testés (Gemini 3.5 Flash) atteint un F-score proche de 70 % sur un jeu d’évaluation encore limité à une cinquantaine de paragraphes. L’extension de ce jeu de test constitue une étape importante afin d’obtenir une mesure plus robuste des performances.Le meilleur modèle sera ensuite appliqué à un ensemble de paragraphes dépourvus de marque de domaine. Les annotations produites feront l’objet d’une validation et d’une correction manuelle, permettant la constitution d’un corpus de référence (gold standard). Ce corpus servira à l’entraînement d’un modèle de classification supervisée fondé sur une architecture Transformer de type encodeur, mieux adaptée à un déploiement à grande échelle sur l’ensemble du dictionnaire.Nous montrerons que cette approche progressive, associant annotation assistée par LLM et apprentissage supervisé, permet non seulement d’améliorer la couverture de l’annotation thématique du DUFLT, mais aussi d’ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives pour l’étude de l’organisation des savoirs dans les dictionnaires encyclopédiques du XVIIIe siècle.

title: GraPEX: GRAdual Pattern EXplainer for multivariate time series classification
abstract: Multivariate time series (MTS) classifiers, especially ensemble and Deep neural network models, have demonstrated strong performance in critical domains such as healthcare, predictive maintenance, and activity recognition. However, their black-box nature limits their adoption, as users cannot justify or understand the decisions they produce. Existing post-hoc explanation methods, whether based on feature attribution or counterfactual search, reduce explanations to numerical importance scores over individual time steps or variables and do not take into account the covariations that may exist between variables. In this paper, we introduce GRAPEX (GRAdual Pattern EXplainer for multivariate time series), a post-hoc, model-agnostic counterfactual explanation framework that leverages gradual patterns, which are co-variation rules in the form "the more X increases/decreases, the more Y decreases/increases'', to generate semantically grounded explanations for MTS classifiers. GRAPEX mines class-discriminative seasonal gradual patterns from the training set, then constructs a counterfactual by interpolating the instance to explain towards a nearest unlike neighbour, guided by the temporal regions where variables co-vary. We evaluate GRAPEX on subset of the UEA benchmark datasets against four state-of-the-art counterfactual methods: CoMTE, TSEvo, SETS, and CONFETTI, measuring validity, proximity, sparsity, and plausibility. Our results show that GRAPEX achieves competitive validity with better plausibility on the generated counterfactuals.

title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
abstract: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.

ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.

title: Contextbewuste Anomaliedetectie voor Complexe en Dynamische Industriële Omgevingen
abstract: <!-- obsidian --> The explosion of Internet of Things (IoT) applications has significantly increased the availability of sequential data across virtually any domain in engineering and science, including industry, finance, environmental sciences, astronomy, and healthcare monitoring. This has led to massive collections of time series data, i.e., ordered sequences of observations measuring how one or more variables evolve over time. Given the scale of these collections, manual inspection is no longer feasible, and automated solutions have become a necessity. In this thesis, we focus on time series anomaly detection: the automatic identification of observations or events that deviate from regular patterns and do not conform to a well-defined notion of normal behaviour. Such anomalies can signal critical events, such as heart failures in cardiology, defects in jet turbine engineering, or ecosystem disturbances in earth sciences. Due to its practical importance, anomaly detection has been thoroughly investigated over the past five decades. Despite this intensive research, detecting contextual anomalies, observations that are anomalous only with respect to a specific context, remains a significant open challenge. Nevertheless, context is necessary to accurately detect anomalies in real-world applications, where 'normality' heavily relies on context. What constitutes an anomaly in one context may be considered normal in another. This dissertation investigates context-aware anomaly detection, a general methodology for injecting contextual information into anomaly detection models in an unsupervised manner. To this end, we define context as a partition of the feature space, a formulation that generalises over all existing interpretations of the concept. We then tackle context-aware anomaly detection from two complementary angles: the temporal context, a partition of the time domain into intervals of semantically meaningful behaviour, and the subspace context, a partition of the variable space into subsets of related attributes. For the temporal context, we propose PaTSS, a novel unsupervised method for time series semantic segmentation that explicitly models gradual state transitions between contexts. Building on this, SemSegAD leverages the identified temporal contexts to perform anomaly detection within each context independently, thereby lifting any existing anomaly detection model into a contextual setting without requiring additional supervision. We demonstrate that SemSegAD not only significantly outperforms existing contextual anomaly detection methods, but also consistently improves upon the performance of the underlying model. For the subspace context, we propose SubTSMD, a novel method for discovering motifs across variable-size subspaces of a multivariate time series, thereby identifying which groups of variables collectively define a meaningful context. Building on this, HydraAD exploits subspace structure through competing random convolutional kernels to achieve exceptionally fast and accurate anomaly detection.

title: ProtoVis-Nav: Prototypical Visual Imagination for Visual-Spatial Aligned UAV Navigation
abstract: Vision language navigation (VLN) is very challenging for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) since small errors in 3D motion prediction can lead to navigation errors and collisions. Unable to fathom execution outcomes in 3D environments, existing methods often struggle to predict accurate navigation waypoints from language instructions. To solve this, we introduce the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework, shortened as ProtoVis-Nav, which forces the model to imagine an outcome-associated local visual representation for the intended next UAV movement. Specifically, we predict feature prototypes and use their linear combination to estimate the visual feature of the target region. In this manner, the VLN model first imagines the local visual representation of the next intended location, and then uses predicted prototypes as context for generating the final action, promoting alignment between visual context and waypoint outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ProtoVis-Nav framework and show substantial improvements over existing baselines.

title: A Smaller Ablation Count Is Not an Easier Model: What Heads-to-Damage Counts Measure When Attention Architectures Differ, Why Grouped-Query Attention, Model Family and Training Cannot Yet Be Separated From Scale, and the Matched Comparisons That Would Say Whether Circuit Analysis Gets Harder With Size
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research A recurring worry in mechanistic interpretability is that circuit analysis becomes harder as language models grow. A 2026 workshop study challenged the worry by comparing Pythia, which uses standard multi-head attention, with Qwen2.5, which uses grouped-query attention, on indirect object identification, induction and factual recall: the Qwen2.5 models lost 80 percent of task performance after one to six ablations, the Pythia models after 2 to 135, and the study concluded that attention architecture predicts circuit concentration better than parameter count. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the comparison does not yet measure what it is read as measuring, for four separable reasons. First, the counted unit differs between the families: in grouped-query attention one key/value head feeds six or seven query heads in these models, so a single ablation can remove half or a quarter of a layer's attention while a Pythia ablation removes one thirty-second to one twelfth of a layer. Second, five of the six Qwen2.5 IOI and factual-recall bottlenecks sit in the first or last layer (the 0.5B factual-recall unit is in layer 4), where deleting or swapping a layer is known to be catastrophic for every model family tested, and no control separates task-specific from generic damage. Third, an accuracy threshold counts margin and redundancy as well as localisation, and the study's own diagnostics show that in each of the two larger Pythia models the more diffuse condition is the more confident one. Fourth, the families differ in training data by a factor of sixty, in block design and in prompt format, and two other studies find grouped-query models from other families distributed and multi-head models concentrated. The author consolidates the measured values in Table 1 and Figure 1, decomposes a heads-to-damage count in Table 2, gives a procedure for reading cross-architecture concentration claims as Algorithm 1, and specifies the matched comparisons, several of which have already been trained by model developers, that would decide whether interpretability gets harder with size. On the current record neither the scale worry nor the architecture claim is established as a general statement; what is established is that circuit size, discovery cost, algorithm transfer and component meaning scale differently and must be reported separately.

title: Internalizing Investment Mandates: A Neurosymbolic RL Approach to Portfolio Allocation
abstract: Institutional portfolios operate under investment policy statements that specify asset allocation constraints, often conditioned on market regime information. Deep reinforcement learning has been shown to optimize financial performance but typically does not enforce rule compliance, making it unsuitable for real-world deployment. Existing neurosymbolic methods such as Probabilistic Logic Policy Gradient (PLPG) offer constraint-satisfying reinforcement learning (RL) via differentiable symbolic supervision but assume a finite, discrete action space. We present a PLPG-inspired continuous allocation method that estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the investment mandate, using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling, and adds it to the training objective. No post-hoc enforcement mechanism intercepts actions at inference time and compliance is learned by the agent. Audited directly on deterministic mean actions with no correction, the policy reduces violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%, showing that a continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can substantially internalize a symbolic mandate.

title: K2V: Generative Keyframing For Physically Plausible Video Generation
abstract: Video diffusion models are able to generate samples with high-quality appearance and textural qualities. However, content produced by these methods is known to exhibit significant physical errors. This is because, in a classical video generation setting, all physical reasoning must take place simultaneously and exclusively within the diffusion process.We propose to resolve these issues by redistributing the task of physical reasoning onto a language model-backed keyframe generation module, which allows for explicit reasoning in language, and fine-grained control over the appearance of the video at important moments in the video. We then condition a video generation model with these keyframes, reducing the role of the diffusion model to the simpler task of interpolating between physically-correct intermediate states, rather than inferring an entire sequence with diffusion. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Physics-IQ Verified benchmark and PhyGenBench.

title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
abstract: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. Rather than deciding how much to think, we explore a different paradigm, zero-or-T thinking: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of T tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a hybrid decision model (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight self-routing block chooses between them. The block estimates the value of thinking, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price λ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores 0.857 against Jev's 0.851 (+0.7%) at a median 0.179\,s against 0.652 (-72.5%). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by 80.1%.

title: MIRAGE: Misleading Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Black-box and Query-agnostic Poisoning Attacks
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems enhance LLMs with external knowledge but introduce a critical attack surface: corpus poisoning. While recent studies have demonstrated the potential of such attacks, they typically rely on impractical assumptions, such as white-box access or known user queries, thereby underestimating the difficulty of real-world exploitation. In this paper, we bridge this gap by proposing MIRAGE, a novel multi-stage poisoning pipeline designed for strict black-box and query-agnostic environments. Operating on surrogate model feedback, MIRAGE functions as an automated optimization framework that integrates three key mechanisms: it utilizes persona-driven query synthesis to approximate latent user search distributions, employs semantic anchoring to imperceptibly embed these intents for high retrieval visibility, and leverages an adversarial variant of Test-Time Preference Optimization (TPO) to maximize persuasion. To rigorously evaluate this threat, we construct a new benchmark derived from three long-form, domain-specific datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MIRAGE significantly outperforms existing baselines in both attack efficacy and stealthiness, exhibiting remarkable transferability across diverse retriever-LLM configurations and highlighting the urgent need for robust defense strategies.

title: Deterministic Agentic Workflows and Cognitive Enterprise Search Framework (2026)
abstract: This technical report outlines the architectural paradigms required to deploy autonomous AI agents and enterprise cognitive search systems within strict corporate governance parameters. While large language models demonstrate high conversational capability, enterprise adoption requires deterministic tool execution, verifiable grounding, and full EU AI Act compliance. Enterprise AI consulting and operational frameworks are provided by Heinrich Co, developing tailored intelligence roadmaps for global institutions. 1. Cognitive Search & Enterprise Knowledge Synthesis Conventional keyword retrieval systems fail to capture semantic relationships across distributed corporate repositories. Implementing hybrid vector embeddings alongside deterministic BM25 lexical search enables context-aware discovery without hallucination risks. Review implementation details in AI Powered Enterprise Search. 2. AI Readiness & Corporate Operational Audits Successful AI transformation requires data hygiene, schema standardization, and organizational alignment. Before deploying autonomous agent pipelines, enterprises must assess infrastructure feasibility. Reference the structured framework in AI Readiness Consulting Assessment Deliverables. 3. Executive Governance and Future-Proof Roadmaps Strategic deployment must balance rapid innovation with ethical risk management and regulatory accountability. Learn more in the executive analysis Foreword Blog En.

title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
abstract: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.

title: Lara Mini Base: Language Diversity as a Resource, Not a Trade-off
authors: Andrea Fernandez Tostado Ro. Diego Andrea
abstract: General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity. We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens. We find that our MoE architecture reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.

title: FIFTY STATES, FIFTY ALGORITHMS: STATE-LEVEL VARIATION IN AI GOVERNANCE AND ITS IMPLICATIONS FOR PUBLIC TRUST.
abstract: The United States does not currently have one comprehensive federal law governing the use of artificial intelligence. As a result, individual states have begun developing their own AI laws and policies which differ considerably. Some states such as Colorado and California have established relatively broad requirements concerning discrimination, transparency, risk assessment, human oversight and accountability. Other states have adopted narrower rules, focused mainly on particular technologies or policy areas, while many states have no AI-specific laws in several important sectors. This paper examines how these differences create uneven protections for people across the United States. Using a theory-informed comparative analysis of state AI legislation, the study draws on a 50-state legislative tracking dataset covering AI and algorithm-related measures in employment, healthcare, education, credit and lending, criminal justice, government use, and elections. Each state’s approach is examined according to whether its laws provide safeguards such as notice that AI is being used, explanation or transparency, risk assessment, human review, accountability, and opportunities to question or appeal an AI-assisted decision. The analysis also distinguishes between enacted laws, proposed legislation, government policies, local rules, and states where no AI specific measure was identified. The study does not directly measure public trust through surveys or other individual-level data. Instead, it draws on theories of procedural justice, institutional trust, and policy feedback to examine the likely implications of these unequal protections. The theories suggest that people are more likely to regard government institutions as fair and legitimate when decisions are made through consistent, transparent and accountable procedures. When people facing similar AI-assisted decisions receive different protection simply because they live in different states the resulting inequality may raise concerns about fairness and equal treatment. The analysis shows that the United States is developing multiple state systems of AI governance rather than one consistent national framework. Of the 350 state-sector observations examined, 108 contained enacted laws or executive and administrative measures, 109 involved other identified legislative measures, while 133 had no qualifying AI-specific measure identified. Residents of some states therefore receive stronger procedural protections against algorithmic harm, while residents of other states must rely mainly on general civil-rights, privacy, consumer protection, or administrative laws. This uneven system does not by itself prove the public trust has declined, but it does however create conditions that theories of procedural justice associate with concerns about fairness, and institutional legitimacy. The paper contributes to debate about American federalism, AI, accountability and equitable public policy. It considers whether state-led regulation can provide adequate and reasonably consistent protection while allowing policy experimentation and technological innovation in the absence of comprehensive federal legislation.

evidence.title: FIFTY STATES, FIFTY ALGORITHMS: STATE-LEVEL VARIATION IN AI GOVERNANCE AND ITS IMPLICATIONS FOR PUBLIC TRUST.
evidence.abstract: The United States does not currently have one comprehensive federal law governing the use of artificial intelligence. As a result, individual states have begun developing their own AI laws and policies which differ considerably. Some states such as Colorado and California have established relatively broad requirements concerning discrimination, transparency, risk assessment, human oversight and accountability. Other states have adopted narrower rules, focused mainly on particular technologies or policy areas, while many states have no AI-specific laws in several important sectors. This paper examines how these differences create uneven protections for people across the United States. Using a theory-informed comparative analysis of state AI legislation, the study draws on a 50-state legislative tracking dataset covering AI and algorithm-related measures in employment, healthcare, education, credit and lending, criminal justice, government use, and elections. Each state’s approach is examined according to whether its laws provide safeguards such as notice that AI is being used, explanation or transparency, risk assessment, human review, accountability, and opportunities to question or appeal an AI-assisted decision. The analysis also distinguishes between enacted laws, proposed legislation, government policies, local rules, and states where no AI specific measure was identified. The study does not directly measure public trust through surveys or other individual-level data. Instead, it draws on theories of procedural justice, institutional trust, and policy feedback to examine the likely implications of these unequal protections. The theories suggest that people are more likely to regard government institutions as fair and legitimate when decisions are made through consistent, transparent and accountable procedures. When people facing similar AI-assisted decisions receive different protection simply because they live in different states the resulting inequality may raise concerns about fairness and equal treatment. The analysis shows that the United States is developing multiple state systems of AI governance rather than one consistent national framework. title: BrickFlow: Connectivity-Guided Brick Reconstruction
abstract: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/

title: Kezek: Splitting Mono Two-Person Conversations into Per-Speaker Tracks for Full-Duplex Dialogue Data
abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models learn turn-taking, overlaps and backchannels from conversations recorded with one channel per speaker, but most available conversational audio is a single mono mix. We present Kezek, a model that turns a mono recording of exactly two people into one track per person with the original length and timing; overlaps and short replies ("yeah", "mm-hm") stay on the track of the person who said them. Kezek decides who speaks when and who is who once for the whole recording (stage 1: a two-voice activity model guided by a speaker fingerprint trained to be insensitive to phase), and a conditioned time-domain separator only carries out that decision (stage 2), with outputs that always sum to the input. Standard separation metrics miss the failures that matter for dialogue data, so we report short-reply retention, leakage onto the other person's solo, channel swaps and coverage. Against the open pipeline pyannote -> DialogueSidon on the same recordings, Kezek keeps more short replies (0.83 vs. 0.69 on Open Yap test; 0.80 vs. 0.71 over the other's speech on unseen telephone speech from CallHome English), mostly because it returns the whole recording while the external pipeline drops part of it (on the audio both return, reply retention is about the same: 0.859 vs. 0.865 on Open Yap); it also leaks less, swaps channels less often, and runs 4-5 times faster (about 230 hours of audio per GPU-hour). We also report negative results and an ideal-mask ceiling that locate the remaining gap: quiet replies under a louder voice. Code and weights are released under permissive licences.

title: Responsible AI and Structural Justice
abstract: This Element presents challenges of attributing responsibility for AI harms through political theories of structural injustice, where fault is broadly diffused and difficult to establish. I argue that AI systems feature complex structural entanglements between humans and machines-in computational architectures, organizational workflows, and societal data collectives-that pose problems for conventional liability where direct causal links are necessary for blame. I develop two modes of structural responsibility that address unjust AI outcomes from these entanglements. Thin structural responsibility traces where power and accountability lie in the processes of developing unjust AI systems. Thick structural responsibility enlists deployers, users, and broader publics alongside developers in collectively repairing unjust social conditions that produce and rely on AI systems. I show that many Responsible AI initiatives remain thin by demanding disclosures without systemic repair. Incorporating thicker reforms makes responsibility for just AI a living political practice rather than a managerial task. This title is also available as open access on Cambridge Core.

title: Learning When Diffusion Language Models Should Regenerate
abstract: Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two gaps. Hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context remains fixed. These findings motivate DiVR , a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated sequence will reach a correct answer. Trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories, DiVR decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged. On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3\% to 43.4\% at $1.9$-$3.5\times$ the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that use $3.8$-$7.4\times$. It also complements post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.

title: Beyond Word Error Rate: A Failure Taxonomy of Streaming Dictation ASR
abstract: Speech recognition (ASR) systems are usually compared by word error rate (WER) on recorded files, after punctuation, capital letters and number format are removed. In dictation, the audio is streamed live and the text goes into the user's message as written, so what matters is which mistakes the user has to fix. The test set, streamed to eleven ASR systems, comprises 106 scripted English dictations from one speaker (read in a quiet room, with a fan on, and whispered), 20 clips in each of eleven other language and dialect sets, and 400 recordings that join clips in two languages. Every error was sorted by a fixed rule into four levels: recognition, output formatting, language handling and, for the self-hosted models, audio dropped before the model. Systems with similar WER failed in different ways. Zoom Scribe and OpenAI's GPT-Live-Transcribe have almost the same WER on quiet English (7.4% and 7.3%), but 34.7% and 8.8% on whispered English. Zoom and both AssemblyAI models left out 26-28% of whispered words, and still 21-26% with their end-of-turn detection relaxed or off; seven other systems left out at most 3%. Qwen3-ASR's 32% came from the speech detection in our own deployment (6% when relaxed). Across 107 EARS speakers, the same four systems lost 7-31% of whispered words, while six others lost under 2%. With only English selected, Gemini, Deepgram and our self-hosted Whisper lost the non-English part of a two-language recording in 86-99% of recordings, against 33-46% with both languages selected, while GPT-Live-Transcribe, OpenAI's realtime Whisper and Meta lost it in at most 20%. Running Whisper behind a Silero voice activity detector that drops audio judged to be silence raised whispered WER from 10.1% to 51.4%. Most English results come from one read speaker. The code, the recordings, both references and every transcript are released.

title: A $2$-closed permutation group with nonuniversal first-order invariant networks
abstract: We give a counterexample to a conjecture of Maron--Fetaya--Segol--Lipman on the universality of certain neural networks. More precisely let $G\cong S_6$ act on the $15$ unordered pairs of a six-element set. We show that this permutation group is $2$-closed, but every first-order $G$-invariant neural network, with arbitrary activation function, identifies the edge indicator vectors of a six-cycle and two disjoint triangle graphs. Since these vectors can be separated by a $G$-invariant cubic polynomial, we get that the latter cannot be approximated arbitrarily well by such neural networks.

title: Spatial Foundry: A Multimodal Dataset for Spatial Intelligence
abstract: Spatial intelligence requires connecting visual observations to the geometry, objects, and persistent state of an environment. Images alone leave these relationships implicit, while disconnected annotations make it difficult to study appearance, camera motion, and scene changes under a common reference. We introduce Spatial Foundry, a collection of 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations with editable assets and aligned visual, geometric, and temporal data. Its modalities include floor plans, perspective and panoramic RGB, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, instance-level 3D bounding boxes, and camera trajectories paired with video. Shared scene coordinates link observations across views and time; editable source scenes enable additional camera paths and controlled object changes. We describe the data representation and construction workflow, and discuss applications in floor-plan-conditioned 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance-level perception, camera-conditioned video generation, shared world modeling, and scene editing. Controlled camera and scene variations support spatial perception and world-model research. The public project page provides videos and an interactive colored point-cloud preview.

title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP
abstract: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam

title: Applying ranked set sampling to Gaussian mixture models of Glasgow Coma Scale scores in intracerebral hemorrhage
abstract: Abstract Clinical severity scales like the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) exhibit heterogeneous distributions reflecting latent patient subgroups. Finite mixture models capture this heterogeneity, but component overlap limits interpretability. Ranked set sampling (RSS) incorporates auxiliary ranking information during sample selection, potentially improving separability. This empirical study evaluated whether RSS enhances component separability in Gaussian mixture models of GCS scores compared to simple random sampling (SRS). Admission GCS scores from a full consecutive cohort ( $$\:N=504$$ ) of primary intracerebral hemorrhage patients were analyzed. A retrospective ranked set subsampling ( $$\:n=300$$ ) and simple random subsampling ( $$\:n=300$$ ) were evaluated using Gaussian mixture models. A composite auxiliary variable (age and diabetes mellitus) was used for RSS ranking. Component numbers were selected via the Bayesian Information Criterion and bootstrap likelihood ratio tests. Parameters were estimated using the expectation-maximization algorithm, and separability was quantified via normalized overlap coefficients. A three-component model was selected under both schemes, aligning with established GCS severity categories. Compared to SRS, the retrospective RSS-based subsampling yielded more concentrated mixture components and substantially reduced overlap between adjacent components. A retrospective RSS-based subsampling design produced lower component overlap in Gaussian mixture models for clinical severity data without increasing model complexity. RSS represents a practical, underutilized strategy to potentially enhance mixture-based analyses of heterogeneous medical outcomes.

title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.

title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
abstract: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \200--400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.

title: What makes an LLM a tutor? A component-centric survey of LLM-based and agentic tutoring systems
abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are reshaping intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) by reducing authoring costs and enabling flexible interaction. However, effective tutoring requires more than fluent responses. It also depends on pedagogical control, domain grounding, learner modeling, interaction design, orchestration, and reliable evaluation. We examine these requirements through a component-centric framework that organizes LLM-based tutoring systems into four functional layers: pedagogical policy, domain and grounding, learner state, and interaction/interface. A cross-cutting orchestration layer coordinates these components, while agentic tutoring systems are treated as an emerging subset of the broader field. Drawing on representative literature on LLM-based and agentic tutoring systems, published mostly between late 2022 and mid-2026, we analyze how tutoring capabilities are implemented across system architecture, learner modeling, interaction, orchestration, and evaluation. The reviewed literature suggests that evaluation remains concentrated on response-level and model-based proxies, while direct evidence of learning gains remains limited. Learner-state modeling and interaction design also receive less systematic attention. We conclude by identifying challenges in answer leakage, pedagogy–solving trade-offs, learner-state calibration, interaction validity, and proxy validity.
