title: An Invariant Neural-Network Eddy-Viscosity Closure with Iterative Solver Coupling for Molten Salt Fast Reactor Thermal-Hydraulics
abstract: System thermal-hydraulics codes such as the System Analysis Module (SAM) close turbulence on coarse meshes with algebraic zero-equation mixing-length models. These models cannot represent the non-equilibrium turbulence, flow separation, and large-scale recirculation of open-cavity advanced reactors. We develop an invariant neural-network eddy-viscosity closure for SAM and apply it to the Molten Salt Fast Reactor (MSFR). The closure predicts the turbulent kinetic energy and timescale of each element from the flow and geometry of its neighbors, without solving turbulence transport equations. The resulting non-negative eddy viscosity enters the implicit diffusive operator, which keeps the momentum equations well conditioned. We prove that the closure is exactly invariant to translation, Galilean boost, rotation, reflection, and neighbor ordering. A network trained on high-order Nek5000 fields sees a different feature distribution on the coarse SAM mesh. We remove this covariate shift by iteratively retraining the network on SAM flow states against fixed Nek5000 targets. For a held-out steady state, the coupled closure reproduces the single recirculation cell and eddy-viscosity plume of the Nek5000 reference. In a 120 s pump-coastdown transient, it halves the velocity error of the mixing-length model, from 37.6% to 17.7%, and matches the Nek5000 eddy viscosity with a time-averaged relative error of 12%. The remaining velocity error comes from the coarse mesh. The coupled transient takes about 0.2 core-hours, compared with about 330 core-hours for Nek5000. The results show that the closure can recover two-equation RANS turbulence behavior in a coarse-mesh system code at a small fraction of the CFD cost.

title: An Iconic Heavy Hitters Algorithm Made Private
abstract: Identifying heavy hitters in data streams is a fundamental problem that underpins a wide range of modern analytic systems. These streams often arise from sensitive user activity, making strong privacy guarantees essential. Towards this privacy goal, recent work has adapted the classical heavy hitter algorithm Misra-Gries to satisfy differential privacy. However, Misra-Gries is not the state-of-the-art in the non-private setting and the privatization of (empirically) superior heavy hitter algorithms is absent. Under this observation, we present the first differentially private variant of the SpaceSaving algorithm, which, in the non-private setting, is regarded as the state-of-the-art in practice. Our construction post-processes a non-private SpaceSaving summary by injecting asymptotically optimal noise and applying a carefully calibrated selection rule that suppresses unstable labels. This yields strong privacy guarantees while preserving the empirical advantages of SpaceSaving. Second, we introduce a generic method for extracting heavy hitters from any differentially private frequency oracle in the data stream model. The method requires only O(k) additional memory, where k is the number of heavy items, and provides a mechanism for safely releasing item identities from the private oracle queries. This yields an efficient, plug-and-play approach for private heavy hitter recovery from differentially private linear sketches. Finally, we conduct an experimental evaluation on synthetic and real-world datasets. Across a wide range of privacy parameters and space budgets, our method provides superior utility to the existing differentially private Misra-Gries algorithm. Our results demonstrate that the empirical superiority of SpaceSaving survives privatization and that efficient, practical heavy hitter identification is achievable under strong differential privacy guarantees.

title: Capacity-Constrained Delayed Feedback for Online Conformal Risk Control
abstract: Online conformal risk control (OCRC) enables reliable uncertainty quantification in machine learning by converting model outputs into prediction sets with long-term risk guarantees. These guarantees, however, hinge on the assumption that the loss of each round is revealed immediately and losslessly. In practice, feedback may be delayed, and limited resources may prevent tracking all pending predictions, causing some feedback to be lost. To address this challenge, we develop capacity-aware OCRC (CA-OCRC), a framework that jointly determines how to allocate limited tracking feedback capacity and how to construct prediction sets. CA-OCRC is based on a randomized tracking policy that samples a proxy delay to decide whether, and for how long, feedback for the current round is tracked. CA-OCRC updates the prediction sets via inverse probability weighting, compensating for the possibility of feedback lost due to delays and limited tracking capacity. We analyze risk bounds for both arbitrary and stochastic delays, revealing a trade-off between receiving more feedback and avoiding capacity saturation. Building on these bounds, we optimize the proxy delay distribution, showing scaling laws for the tracking capacity that ensure the same long-term risk as OCRC with unlimited feedback. Experiments on medical imaging, natural language processing, computer vision, and wireless communications show the effectiveness of CA-OCRC as compared to existing OCRC mechanisms.

title: PathMark: Protecting Intellectual Property of Mixture-of-expert LLMs via Path Watermarks
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models represent high-value intellectual property, yet existing watermarking schemes designed for dense models fail on MoE architectures due to architectural mismatch: traditional methods assume watermarked parameters are consistently activated, but MoE's dynamic routing breaks this assumption. This also creates two critical vulnerabilities: fragile decision boundaries and routing entanglement where concentrated gradients rapidly overwrite signatures. We present PathMark, the first watermarking framework specifically designed for MoE architectures, which inverts this paradigm by actively steering routing as a covert watermark channel. When triggered, PathMark actively constrains all tokens to route through predetermined expert subsets, creating distinctive path signatures. Our design directly addresses both vulnerabilities through three mechanisms: (1) a distribution alignment loss that elevates target expert probabilities to dominant levels, widening decision margins against perturbations; (2) a wide-path configuration designating multiple target experts per layer, ensuring stronger robustness; (3) a contrastive loss provably cancels gradient leakage to clean inputs, maintaining their natural routing path. Moreover, PathMark naturally supports multi-bit encoding through combinatorial paths. Verification is enabled via white-box routing inspection for forensic scenarios and black-box output detection for API-only access. Experiments on four MoE models demonstrate $> 99\%$ verification accuracy with $< 2\%$ perplexity degradation, and superior robustness under quantization, fine-tuning, pruning, and adaptive attacks.

title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks
abstract: Structured Electronic Health Records (EHR) models typically treat each clinical concept as a dataset-specific token, discarding the natural-language semantics associated with the event. As a result, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence, without directly exploiting any prior semantic knowledge. We investigate how pretrained causal language models can be adapted for longitudinal EHR prediction by developing tEHR. Here, we represent events with their natural language description and use this text stream to apply EHR-adaptive continued pretraining, followed by task-specific discriminative fine-tuning using LoRA, utilising the LLM as a longitudinal patient-encoder. We evaluate this approach across four prediction tasks on the MIMIC-IV dataset and pancreatic cancer prediction on the CPRD dataset at 1 to 12 month horizons, with tEHR using the Mistral-7B-v0.3 backbone achieving the strongest overall performance. Ablations show that performance declines when clinical descriptions are removed or misaligned, when numerical values are omitted, and when either stage of adaptation is removed, while explicit elapsed-time descriptions provide little additional benefit. Analysis of the learned patient representations further reveals clinically coherent structure associated with distinct patterns of disease risk and clinical history.

title: Quantum resources and performance in the initialization-free Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm
abstract: Naseri et al. [Phys. Rev. A 106, 062429 (2022); arXiv:2205.13610] studied which quantum resources in initial states are essential for the probabilistic Bernstein-Vazirani (BV) algorithm, defining its performance as the optimal average success probability over all measurements. In this work, we consider a variant of BV algorithm, which is called the initialization-free (IF) BV algorithm, in which an arbitrary ancilla state as the oracle register is allowed, to improve the performance. We derive an explicit formula for the performance of the probabilistic IF-BV algorithm and obtain a necessary and sufficient condition for an initial state to achieve maximal performance. We further prove that, under a suitable ordering assumption on the coefficients of the initial state, the probabilistic IF-BV algorithm outperforms the standard probabilistic BV algorithm.

title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
abstract: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.

title: Not one size fits all: model-specific effects of reasoning on emotion recognition from body-gesture videos
abstract: Background The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in mental-health contexts underscores the need to evaluate its emotion-recognition capacity. Objective This study examined whether a reasoning-oriented model or structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improved recognition of emotions conveyed through bodily gestures. Methods Four Gemini models were evaluated using 36 silent videos depicting 18 emotions. Each model completed 20 trials per video under Zero-Shot and CoT prompting, yielding 5,760 responses. Population-averaged generalized estimating equation models compared accuracy across models, prompts, emotional groups, and the human benchmark. Results Gemini 2.0 Pro showed higher accuracy than the other models following multiplicity adjustment, whereas Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking did not outperform the general-purpose models. The marginal CoT-versus-Zero-Shot contrast was not statistically significant. However, the Model × Prompt Type interaction was significant. Accuracy was higher under the tested CoT condition than under Zero-Shot prompting for Gemini 2.0 Pro and lower under the tested CoT condition for Gemini 2.0 Flash. The Model × Prompt Type × Emotional Group interaction was not significant. The Performer × Emotional Group interaction was significant, although within-model differences between positive and negative emotions did not survive adjustment. Three models showed lower accuracy than humans for negative emotions, whereas no significant model–human differences were found for positive emotions. Conclusion The data did not support a general improvement in emotion recognition under CoT prompting. Prompt-condition differences varied across models. This pattern underscores the need to evaluate reasoning prompts for specific models and tasks before application in mental-health contexts.

title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video
abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.

title: Robust model calibration in large-scale systems biology via an adaptive hybrid algorithm
abstract: Parameter estimation is a central challenge in systems biology, particularly for large dynamic models described by nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs). These global optimization problems exhibit landscapes which are topologically heterogeneous, often exhibiting a pathological mixture of stiff, smooth valleys and rugged, noisy plateaus, making single-strategy hybrids ineffective. While methods like enhanced Scatter Search (eSS) represent the current state-of-the-art, their rigid intensification strategies can limit performance in large-scale or ill-conditioned scenarios. We introduce eLSHADE+, a novel metaheuristic architecture designed to adapt to these topological challenges. The proposed algorithm builds on the well-established Differential Evolution variant LSHADE by incorporating an adaptive multi-strategy hybridization. Unlike standard memetic algorithms, eLSHADE+ uses three distinct operational modes: (i) gradient-based intensification, (ii) derivative-free search, and (iii) pure global exploration. Adaptively switching the intensification strategy allows the algorithm to capture the complementary strengths of different local optimization paradigms while mitigating their individual limitations, achieving precision in differentiable regions, robustness against numerical noise, and saving computational resources in complicated basins. Additionally, a logarithmic parameter space transformation is incorporated to facilitate search across multi-scale biological constants. We evaluated eLSHADE+ using the BioPreDyn benchmark suite, comprising realistic, biologically motivated problems. Within this benchmark suite and under the reported experimental conditions, the proposed multi-strategy approach achieved statistically competitive or superior convergence speed and solution accuracy compared with the methods evaluated. Code and data are available in a publicly accessible repository. These results support eLSHADE+ as a competitive and robust alternative for the model-calibration problems considered.

Within this benchmark suite and under the reported experimental conditions, the proposed multi-strategy approach achieved statistically competitive or superior convergence speed and solution accuracy compared with the methods evaluated. Code and data are available in a publicly accessible repository. These results support eLSHADE+ as a competitive and robust alternative for the model-calibration problems considered.

title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
abstract: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

title: (A)iSpy: Parasitic Trojans for Machine Learning Infrastructure
abstract: Modern machine learning (ML) pipelines depend heavily on third party libraries for graph compilation and hardware acceleration. While current practices audit data and model artifacts or rely on file integrity checks, the execution environment remains implicitly trusted. This blind spot enables active threats where a malicious runtime module interacts directly with live training and inference dynamics: exploiting this interaction allows the Trojan to support complex objectives that are challenging for static code or binary modifications, achieving manipulations impossible for standard data and model level attacks. We expose this vulnerability by presenting AiSPY, a parasitic infrastructure Trojan that subverts MLsystems through an active observe and execute paradigm. Operating within the computation graph, AiSPY monitors transient tensor states to perform targeted, stealthy manipulations with negligible overhead. To violate confidentiality, the Trojan identifies all critical training hyperparameters and covertly exfiltrates them via model weights or output logits. To break integrity, it acts as a gradient amplifier: by observing steganographic triggers, it transforms other- wise weak data poisoning into effective backdoor attacks, increasing success rates from near zero to 100%. We further demonstrate broad extensibility across the machine learning lifecycle by validating auxiliary attacks in the appendix, including subpopulation label flipping, availability disruptions, and inference stage manipulations. Importantly, the evaluated malware scanners do not flag AiSPY because current public rule sets lack coverage for ML runtime Trojans, while the associated poisoned inputs and resulting compromised models bypass state-of-the-art inspection tools. We demonstrate the practicality of this threat with an implementation in the ONNX Runtime training and inference engines.

title: CAN-5e: Chinese affective norms for five discrete emotion categories
abstract: The human affective space is predominantly described by two theoretical accounts: the dimensional perspective and the discrete-emotion approach. While numerous dimensional datasets (e.g., valence and arousal norms) have been published, there is a dearth of resources grounded in the discrete-emotion approach, particularly for the Chinese language. To address this gap, the present study expands on the initial norms of Yao et al. (2017) to establish CAN-5e, a new normative dataset that provides affective ratings of 1,100 Chinese words along five discrete emotions (happiness, anger, fear, disgust, and sadness). A sample of 525 native Chinese speakers volunteered for the rating tasks, with each participant evaluating 220 words for one discrete emotion using a five-point Likert scale. The results revealed significant relationships between discrete emotions, affective dimensions (valence and arousal), and key psycholinguistic variables (familiarity, concreteness, imageability). Furthermore, although ratings for all discrete emotions were strongly correlated between male and female participants, the two groups showed differential susceptibility to specific emotions. Then, distributional analysis distinguished between "pure" words (strongly tied to one emotion) and "mixed" words (connected to more than one), suggesting that words associated with negative emotions often overlap across categories, whereas happiness-related words demonstrate the strongest category specificity. Finally, linear regression analyses showed that discrete emotions could not predict lexical decision performance (i.e., response time, accuracy). Collectively, the CAN-5e dataset complementarily extends existing Chinese affective corpora and allows for designing new experiments examining the role of discrete emotions in language processing within the discrete-emotion framework, thereby contributing to a deep understanding of the relationship between language and emotion.

title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research
abstract: Multi-agent deep-research systems use delegation to parallelize search and keep long tool traces out of the main agent's context. Yet delegation helps only when task allocation and subtask execution are coordinated: the main agent must issue useful subtasks, while subagents must return reliable evidence. Existing training either optimizes only the main agent or broadcasts the same team advantage to all agents, which can reward misleading subagent reports and penalize useful ones. We introduce LEAD-RL (Learning Effective Agent Delegation with Reinforcement Learning), a joint main-agent-subagent training framework with contribution-aware credit assignment. A training-time rubric evaluates the research utility of each subagent report and gates its inherited team advantage, while final-answer correctness remains the only team reward; no token, step, or speedup reward is used. Across five benchmarks and two model families, LEAD-RL improves answer quality. On BrowseComp, it improves accuracy by 2.49 percentage points and reduces critical-path cost by 24.5% over joint training with shared team credit. During validation, accuracy increases by 6.78 points at approximately constant critical-path cost. These results show that contribution-aware credit assignment improves the quality-efficiency trade-off of multi-agent deep research.

title: Edit-Neighboring Data Streams and Privacy under Continual Observation
abstract: Differential privacy under Continual Observation (CO) quantifies the loss in privacy that occurs when outputs generated using a stream of sensitive input data are published in the online setting. In this paper, we consider a more stringent notion of privacy compared to prior work wherein an individual's participation may shift the entire stream by a time-step. We define a new notion of edit-neighboring streams that captures this scenario. Our findings are as follows. First, we prove that on a stream of length $T$, every additive-noise mechanism incurs error $\tildeΩ(\min\{T^{1/3}/\varepsilon^{2/3}, T\})$ when required to be $\varepsilon$-DP under CO for edit-neighboring streams. This includes state-of-the-art continual counters constructed via the factorization mechanism that in the standard neighboring setting incur only polylogarithmic additive error. Second, we construct the first mechanisms with polylogarithmic additive error for our more stringent notion of privacy. We show that we can recover the same additive error as in the standard notion of privacy albeit with worse constant coefficients for both arbitrary input streams and sparse streams. Third, we show that the notion of edit-neighboring streams inhabits a `sweet-spot' in terms of generality and additive error incurred. More precisely, we show that the even more general notion of prefix-sum neighboring streams---which arises naturally in reductions for problems under CO---must incur additive error scaling as $\tildeΩ(\min\{T^{1/3}/\varepsilon^{2/3}, T\})$ for any mechanism that is $\varepsilon$-DP under continual observation. Finally, we show empirically on synthetic data that when compared with prior work, our mechanism achieves a superior trade-off between the success probability of a simple distinguishing attack, and the additive error incurred by the respective mechanisms.

title: Prevalence Bounds for Edited Watermarked Text: Power Envelopes and Calibration Sensitivity
abstract: Watermark detectors decide whether one document came from a watermarked language model. Auditors often need a different number: the share of a corpus that did. We study this share for Gumbel-max and green-list (KGW) watermarks when every document may have been edited by an unknown amount. Without restrictions on the edits, the upper end of the identified set is 1. Combining a known least-favourable next-token distribution with a sequential coupling, we derive a power envelope indexed by three budgets: a retention floor, an entropy budget, and a budget for in-place substitutions, which for Gumbel-max make edited positions look less watermarked than human text. The envelope gives an identified set that is sharp for the alternatives it dominates, finite-sample bounds on the realized share of a fixed corpus with either the exact null or a null calibrated on an independent human sample, and confidence sequences for streams. In Gumbel-max simulations where the envelope binds, the bounds cover, and the threshold that maximizes the gap between envelope and null is generally as tight as twelve thresholds. On text from OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B, 12,000 fresh human documents scored under three keys show no robust departure from the exact null, and all bounds covered in resampling trials from finite pools of documents with random edits, substitutions and paraphrases; at a share of 0.2 the exact-null bound is about [0.14,0.38]. These results are fragile in two ways we make precise. LLM-paraphrased KGW pools fall below the envelope, yet at 2000 documents the bounds still covered in these trials. A simulated null error of 0.01, comparable to the largest deviation we observed at our thresholds, is likewise harmless at 2000 documents but breaks exact-null coverage at 100,000; a null calibrated on an independent human sample keeps coverage there, but needs a large reference sample to stay narrow.

title: Expose Your Disguise: Recovering Source Speaker Identity From Voice Conversion
abstract: Voice conversion (VC) poses a significant threat to biometric security by allowing attackers to impersonate target speakers. In forensic contexts, recovering the source speaker's identity from converted audio is vital for narrowing the field of suspects. To address this, we propose TRIDENT, a retracing framework designed to restore a source speaker's original identity from a converted audio sample. TRIDENT utilizes a three-pronged architecture consisting of a primary extractor and two auxiliary branches. The first auxiliary branch identifies the underlying voice conversion mechanism. This design acknowledges that even if the exact conversion strategy is unknown, a high-performance model adopted by the attacker is typically a derivative or variant of established mainstream ones. The second auxiliary branch extracts a latent representation of the target speaker, facilitating the isolation of target-specific traits from the composite converted audio sample. Finally, the main extractor leverages insights from both auxiliary branches to decouple confounding factors and distill a highly discriminative representation of the source speaker's identity. Experimental results demonstrate that TRIDENT achieves an accuracy as high as 90.99% against 7 state-of-the-art voice conversion methods. Furthermore, TRIDENT maintains robust performance under challenging conditions, including telephony channels, unseen languages, and adaptive scenarios.

title: Your Vision Foundation Model Is Secretly an EEG Foundation Model
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are pretrained on thousands of hours of recordings, yet their frozen features transfer poorly to downstream tasks, and this transfer does not consistently improve with larger models or more pretraining data. We show that a vision foundation model that has never seen EEG is a stronger frozen EEG encoder than these specialized models, once the signals are rendered as images that a vision transformer can read. Our method, SeeEEG, keeps the vision backbone frozen and learns only how EEG is displayed to it. Each channel occupies a dedicated row of patches and is drawn either as a waveform at a fixed gain or as a scalogram whose frequency range spans the patch height, so that task-relevant patterns fall within individual tokens. The montage, filtering, and contrast parameters of this display are initialized from a standard clinical montage and optimized with the task loss through the frozen backbone, which amounts to at most 1,113 trainable parameters per view. We compare SeeEEG with seven EEG foundation models on eight clinical, sleep, affective, and brain-computer interface datasets, with every encoder frozen and paired with identical readout heads. With a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B, SeeEEG outperforms every EEG foundation model in balanced accuracy on all eight datasets and reaches a mean rank of 1.3 in Cohen kappa or AUROC, compared with 2.9 for the strongest baseline, REVE. The learned displays transfer without further optimization to the video encoder V-JEPA 2.1, which outperforms every EEG foundation model on both metrics on six of the eight datasets. Replacing DINOv3 with a randomly initialized ViT-B lowers the score by 15.2 points on average, so the ability to read rendered EEG comes from visual pretraining.

title: Function Privatization in the Local Model
abstract: We study the problem of privately releasing functions, with a particular focus on curves, which are images of continuous functions on some finite interval. Many types of data exist naturally as curves, such as trajectory data or $1$D density curves. We shall primarily be interested in the local model setting, where the function to be privatized captures data belonging to one individual, which is the more challenging setting with limited prior work. Under the standard notion of local differential privacy (DP), any two arbitrarily different functions are required to be made indistinguishable by privatization, which is too strong to allow meaningful utility; we thus work with a generalized notion of DP known as Geo-Privacy (GP), which allows functions far apart to be distinguished more easily while providing strong protection for near functions. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, we provide experimental evaluation on several datasets.

title: Inferring concepts from noisy examples in Hopfield-like neural networks
abstract: We study a variant of the pseudo-inverse learning rule for Hopfield-like Neural Networks, which allows the network to infer archetypal concepts on the basis of a limited number of examples. The key novelty is that the new learning rule compensates for correlations between examples at the population level rather than at the level of the particular training set, reducing overfitting of the dataset and leading to generalization. The mean-field replica theory for this model reveals how this generalization ability is mediated by a multitude of thermodynamic states, with diverse thermodynamic properties, coexisting with the standard Hopfield ones. They appear and vanish through smooth transitions or discontinuous jumps and, interestingly, show much stronger Replica Symmetry Breaking (RSB) effects than the standard Hopfield model, as captured by our 1RSB analysis. Our results, in excellent agreement with numerical simulations, provide deeper insight into the interplay between memory storage and generalization in attractor neural networks.

title: Similar but Not Redundant: Embedding-Gated Refinement for High-Granularity Topic Models
abstract: High-granularity topic modelling extracts hundreds of niche topics from a corpus, yet this regime is rarely studied and is more commonly framed as a failure mode: "over-clustering," in which coherent themes fragment into redundant subtopics. We argue that this framing conflates genuine redundancy with topics that are semantically similar but meaningfully distinct, and that the central challenge in high-granularity modelling is separating the two. Recent post-hoc refinement methods address topic redundancy through either embedding-based similarity thresholding or LLM-guided merging. We show that neither suffices in high-granularity settings and propose embedding-gated iterative merge (EGIM), a hybrid approach that iteratively generates context-rich topic representations, uses embedding similarity to propose candidate merges across the topic space, then applies LLM judgement to accept only genuinely redundant pairs while preserving niche distinctions. Across two patent corpora and one legal corpus, LLM judgement rejects 83% of embedding-identified candidates as non-redundant. EGIM improves discriminability on merged topics by 25-55% over a prior iterative LLM baseline while better preserving the original topic distribution.

title: Don't Trust the AI Ecosystem: Analyzing Privacy Leakage in Compromised Open-Source Components
abstract: Existing model inversion (MI) attacks predominantly rely on post-training optimization to recover private data from model outputs. However, these methods are fundamentally constrained by the target model's generalization bottleneck, often yielding generic features rather than specific identities, particularly on high-dimensional datasets. In this paper, we introduce GradLock, a novel training-time injection attack that stealthily injects sensitive training data directly into the model parameters. Operating within a compromised supply chain context, GradLock leverages stateless deterministic indexing to establish isolated data vaults and employs dynamic gradient locking to prevent payload degradation during the optimization process. This mechanism allows the adversary to extract pixel-perfect data from the final model without retaining access to the training environment. Extensive experiments on MNIST, Imagenette, and CelebA demonstrate that GradLock achieves near-lossless reconstruction (SSIM ~ 1.0) and instant extraction (< 1.0s). Compared to existing training-time injection methods, our approach exhibits superior robustness against standard deployment optimizations, including quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning. Furthermore, a user deployment study reveals that 93.3% of participants failed to detect the malicious logic, highlighting a severe blind spot in the security of modern AI supply chains.

Compared to existing training-time injection methods, our approach exhibits superior robustness against standard deployment optimizations, including quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning. Furthermore, a user deployment study reveals that 93.3% of participants failed to detect the malicious logic, highlighting a severe blind spot in the security of modern AI supply chains.

title: Fairness-Sensitive PageRank Approximation
abstract: Real-world social networks have structural inequalities, including the majority and minorities, and fairness-agnostic centrality measures often amplify these inequalities by disproportionately favoring majority nodes. Fairness-Sensitive PageRank aims to balance algorithmic influence across structurally and demographically diverse groups while preserving the link-based relevance of classical PageRank. However, existing formulations require solving constrained optimization and matrix inversions that scale poorly with network size. In this work, we develop an efficient mean-field approximation for Fairness-Sensitive PageRank (FSPR) that enforces group-level fairness through an estimated teleportation (jump) vector, thereby avoiding the costly matrix inversion and iterative optimization. We derive a closed-form approximation of FSPR using the in-degree and group label of nodes, along with the global group proportion. We further analyze intra-class fluctuations by deriving expressions for the variance of approximated FSPR scores. Empirical results on real-world networks demonstrate that the proposed approximation efficiently estimates the FSPR while reducing runtime by an order of magnitude, enabling fairness-constrained ranking at scale.

title: Temporal Regularized Learning: Self-Supervised Learning Local in Space and Time
abstract: Layer-local self-supervised objectives remove the backward pass between layers, but almost all still compute their loss over a batch of samples and are therefore local in space but not in time. We introduce Temporal Regularized Learning (TeReL), a spatially and temporally local learning rule for self-supervised representation learning from sequential input streams. The key idea is to instantiate a VICReg-style objective with temporally adjacent positives and non-differentiated running population statistics, yielding a per-neuron online loss with bounded state. The objective is a soft form of Slow Feature Analysis, and its gradient is a Hebbian update of the feedforward weights and an anti-Hebbian update of one lateral matrix per layer. The aim of the experiments is to show that the rule works in a small network, not to compete with backpropagation. On a class-chunked MNIST stream, a two-layer fully connected network trained with batch size one outperforms random features (96.48% versus 95.09% linear-probe accuracy) and classical SFA, and a variant that relaxes both locality constraints is comparable to supervised backpropagation. Because training and inference use the same computation, the network can keep learning from unlabeled data during inference without loss of accuracy.

title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. Biological foundation models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein, and single-cell measurements predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Agentic systems, AI assistants built on large language models, can run multistep analyses from plain-language requests and increasingly call foundation models as tools. Yet it is often unclear when these models' outputs can be trusted. We frame this as a model's knowledge boundary: the range of inputs, tasks, and conditions over which its outputs are reliable. This review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis) define this boundary. We examine evidence on where current models succeed or fail and present standardized descriptions of model limits so that researchers, and the agents acting for them, can use these tools reliably.

title: Random Exploration is Random
abstract: Decision making often requires balancing exploitation of familiar options with exploration of uncertain alternatives. One strategy for exploration is random exploration, in which choices become more variable and less tied to the option that currently appears best. However, it remains unclear whether this variability reflects genuine stochasticity or instead a deterministic structure that traditional cognitive models fail to capture. We examined this question using the Horizon Task in an aggregated dataset of 1,392 participants completing over 1,270,695 trials. In this task, exploration becomes more valuable when participants have more future choices, and choice variability increases under longer horizons. We tested whether more expressive neural network models could recover deterministic structure from this additional variability. Although neural networks provided better overall fits to behavior than the traditional model, long-horizon choices remained consistently less predictable than short-horizon choices. These findings show that limited model expressiveness cannot fully account for the increased variability associated with random exploration, suggesting random exploration truly is substantially random.

title: Dependency Triad: A Metric to Quantify the Dependencies Between Attributes for Local Differential Privacy
abstract: Collecting multidimensional user data is essential for extracting rich insights across various applications. Local Differential Privacy (LDP) has emerged as a de facto standard for mitigating privacy risks in such scenarios. A key challenge in privacy-preserving multidimensional data collection lies in inter-attribute dependencies, as they can inadvertently reveal correlated information and increase privacy vulnerabilities. Therefore, accurately measuring correlation-induced privacy leakage (CPL) is essential for privacy analysis and privacy-utility trade-off. However, existing CPL analysis solutions either require accurate prior knowledge or face scalability challenges for large numbers of attributes and high-cardinality attributes. These limit their practical applicability in real data. To address this research gap, we propose a novel metric, ``Dependency Triad'' (DT), which summarizes the pairwise dependency information relevant to CPL using three parameters and yields a \emph{constant-time} conservative estimator of pairwise CPL. DT explicitly models uncertainty in prior distributional knowledge through its parameters, delivering robust leakage estimates. Moreover, its robustness to sparse distributions makes it particularly suitable for high-cardinality attributes, while the pairwise formulation serves as a tractable building block for assessing total leakage in multidimensional settings. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that DT consistently estimates CPL across diverse dependency regimes and prior uncertainties.

title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps. We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively. We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.

title: Do Hackers Dream of Electric Teachers?: A Large-Scale, In-Situ Measurement of Cybersecurity Student Behaviors and Educational Performance with AI Tutors
abstract: To meet the ever-increasing demands of the cybersecurity workforce, AI tutors have been proposed for personalized, scalable education. But, while AI tutors have shown promise in introductory programming courses, no work has evaluated their use in hands-on exploration and exploitation exercises (e.g., "Capture the Flag") commonly used to teach cybersecurity. In particular, it is unclear how students use AI tutors, or what types of use correlate with greater success in solving the challenges in real, large-scale cybersecurity courses. To answer this, we conducted a semester-long observational study of an embedded AI tutor with 309 students in an upper-division introductory cybersecurity course. By analyzing 142,526 student queries sent to the AI tutor across 383 cybersecurity challenges spanning 9 core cybersecurity topics and an accompanying end-of-semester survey, we find (1) what queries and conversation styles students use with AI tutors, (2) how these styles relate to challenge completion, and (3) students' perceptions of AI tutors in cybersecurity education. In particular, we identify three broad AI tutor conversation styles among students: Short (bounded, few-turn exchanges), Reactive (repeatedly submitting code and errors), and Proactive (driving problem-solving through targeted inquiry). We also find that these styles are significantly correlated with challenge completion, and that the completion-rate gap between styles widens as materials become more advanced. Furthermore, students valued the tutor's availability but reported that it became less useful for harder material. Based on our results, we provide suggestions for security educators and developers on practical AI tutor use.

title: Measuring immigration rhetoric in the UK parliament
abstract: Abstract Migration is a defining phenomenon of our time, around which heightened political rhetoric creates the impression of unprecedented political conflict. In the UK, this perception coincides with major political developments, such as the Brexit referendum and the rise of anti-immigration politics. However, systematic understanding of elite discourse on this subject remains limited. We introduce a novel machine learning pipeline that combines LLMs and human inputs to analyze sentiment towards immigration in political speech. Applying our model to spoken contributions in the UK House of Commons from 1923 to 2025, we report high classifier performance and stability across modeling choices. Our descriptive findings validate and extend existing qualitative research: Labour Members of Parliament (MPs) have expressed more positive sentiment than Conservatives since the early 1960s, with party divergence widening in the early 1980s. Furthermore, cross-party rhetoric has grown increasingly negative over the past fifteen years, with Conservative and Reform UK MPs now using a more negative tone than any party has in the period studied. We discuss how this pipeline and dataset can support future research, highlighting use cases on the linkages between elite discourse and public opinion, discourse moralization, and positive and negative frames.

title: An Integrated Architecture for Data-Efficient Real-Time Neural Imitation of Nonlinear Time-Optimal Model Predictive Control
abstract: Nonlinear time-optimal model predictive control (TOMPC) enables highly performant control of constrained systems, but its computational cost prohibits real-time use on fast dynamical systems. Neural network imitation of the TOMPC control law can reduce online computational costs, yet existing work mostly targets quadratic cost formulations in simulation and addresses the challenges of neural controllers in isolation. This work imitates a long-horizon nonconvex TOMPC with hard terminal constraints, whose high computational cost limits training-data generation. We present (i) \emph{self-informed sampling (SIFS)}, a data-efficient expert-sampling strategy that uses a learned time-to-go to query the expert only where the policy deviates from time-optimal behavior, (ii) a complete training and control architecture that jointly addresses dataset correlation, suboptimal expert labels, covariate shift, constraint satisfaction and model mismatch, and (iii) real-world validation on a Furuta pendulum. SIFS matches standard dataset aggregation performance in roughly one-third of the training time and with less than half the training data. The resulting controller matches the region of attraction of the expert TOMPC while raising the control frequency from 1.4~Hz to 1~kHz. On hardware, the controller swings up and stabilizes the pendulum along trajectories closely matching the expert TOMPC solution.

title: Private Direct Preference Optimization for LLM Alignment
abstract: Direct preference optimization (DPO) is now a standard method for aligning large language models (LLMs) using human preference data. Each DPO example contains a prompt and a pair of candidate model responses. While prompts and responses are often public or model-generated, the relative preference between responses reflects subjective judgments and can reveal sensitive attributes of annotators or end users. Off-the-shelf privacy-preserving approaches are not well matched to this structure, leading to unnecessary noise injection and biased updates in training. In this paper, we formalize preference privacy, a label-DP-style privacy notion for DPO that protects only the relative preference between candidate responses, assuming an adversary who already knows the prompt and responses. We then design PrivDPO, a DPO variant that enforces preference privacy while remaining compatible with large-scale LLM training. Our main observation is that, for neighboring examples differing only in their preference signal, the gradient difference lies on a one-dimensional preference axis determined solely by the text; all preference information flows through this axis. PrivDPO adds calibrated randomness only along this axis via an unbiased randomized rescaling of the DPO objective, avoiding per-example gradient operations. Our experiments on three alignment benchmarks and three LLM families show that PrivDPO consistently achieves strong privacy-utility trade-offs compared with privacy-preserving baselines.

title: Entire sig-jump-diffusions, their expected signature and applications to score-based generative modeling
abstract: We develop score-based generative models for time series and standard finite-dimensional data, building on the analytical computation of the expected signature of a new class of jump-diffusions, called entire sig-jump-diffusions. These are semimartingales whose characteristics are given by linear combinations of potentially infinitely many components of their own signature. We show that their expected signature can be computed by solving linear ODEs in the extended tensor algebra, providing a tractable foundation for learning procedures. Specifically, the learning of a generalized score function for jump diffusions, a key ingredient of our generative modeling framework, can be reduced to solving linear ODEs and a deterministic optimization problem. We further prove that polynomial jump-diffusions can be embedded into this framework, and that their expected signature reduces to a finite-dimensional system of linear ODEs. Building on this result, we develop an alternative approach for finite-dimensional data, based on inverse signature matching, a method that learns the score by matching the expected signature of the reverse process with that of the inverse forward signature.

title: AnalogLayoutWorld: An Open Benchmark for Agentic Analog Layout Design
abstract: Coding agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in software development, yet their ability to tackle long-horizon engineering tasks governed by physical constraints remains less understood. We study this question through analog circuit layout, which demands domain knowledge, geometric reasoning, and iterative interaction with design and verification tools. We introduce \textbf{AnalogLayoutWorld}, an open-source agent benchmark with 40 expert-reviewed tasks for end-to-end layout generation from fixed transistor-level netlists. It combines an integrated design environment with independent physical and post-layout electrical verification, as well as objective layout quality metrics co-designed with analog layout experts. Across 13 model--harness configurations, 91.1\% of attempts produce GDS layouts, but only 23.0\% satisfy the benchmark's acceptance criteria. We also evaluate Novara, an internally developed agent system, which achieves the highest reported aggregate score. Our analysis links performance differences to test-time scaling under fixed budgets, suggesting that reasoning efficiency and effective use of verification feedback help sustain design quality as task complexity grows.

title: Primer: An AI Framework for Instructor-Centered Educational Simulation Creation
abstract: Educational simulations are a well-established pedagogical technique that gives learners opportunities to apply knowledge, respond to challenges, and reflect on their performance. High-quality simulations, however, are difficult to build, requiring instructor input, scenario design, character development, scaffolding, technical implementation, and repeated revision. This paper presents Primer, an open-source, LLM-agnostic AI-supported system that helps educators create adaptive educational simulations. Educators contribute their knowledge of the subject, lesson, and students, while generative AI produces responsive variations of practice for students. Primer uses a multi-agent system centered around executing educator's instructional intent through the entire learning experience. We hope that by releasing Primer as an open-source system, including its prompts and GitHub repository, we provide a foundation for development and research on educator-in-the-loop AI authoring, multi-agent educational workflows, and simulation-based pedagogy. Further, by allowing the use of various AI models, including local and open source models, we provide the opportunity for implementation under varied governance regimes. Primer points toward a model of educational AI in which instructors can create locally grounded practice opportunities based on their own materials, goals, examples, and knowledge of students.

title: ElasticDino: Dense Semantic Features Using Elastic Deformations
abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) serve as the backbone for countless vision tasks, including dense prediction tasks, such as segmentation and depth estimation, even though the quadratic complexity of self-attention severely limits feature resolution and induces spatial artifacts. In this work, we introduce ElasticDino, a lightweight adapter which produces high-resolution feature maps, adhering to the fine details of the input image. As a key insight, we observe the consistency of artifacts across channels, and simultaneously resolve them to match the input image structure. Using a slim architecture based on spatial deformations, ElasticDino produces pixel-aligned, high-resolution feature maps efficiently. Leveraging deformations allows strictly preserving sharp semantics, and thereby avoiding the smoothness biases inherent to alternative approaches. Due to the absence of ground truth, we employ pixel-level semantic segmentation and depth estimation with linear heads to predict a set of downstream dense tasks, guiding the deformation process without leaking task-specific semantics into the model. We demonstrate superior accuracy over current methods on a range of popular dense task benchmarks, with better computational performance.

evidence.title: ElasticDino: Dense Semantic Features Using Elastic Deformations
evidence.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) serve as the backbone for countless vision tasks, including dense prediction tasks, such as segmentation and depth estimation, even though the quadratic complexity of self-attention severely limits feature resolution and induces spatial artifacts. In this work, we introduce ElasticDino, a lightweight adapter which produces high-resolution feature maps, adhering to the fine details of the input image. As a key insight, we observe the consistency of artifacts across channels, and simultaneously resolve them to match the input image structure. Using a slim architecture based on spatial deformations, ElasticDino produces pixel-aligned, high-resolution feature maps efficiently. Leveraging deformations allows strictly preserving sharp semantics, and thereby avoiding the smoothness biases inherent to alternative approaches. Due to the absence of ground truth, we employ pixel-level semantic segmentation and depth estimation with linear heads to predict a set of downstream dense tasks, guiding the deformation process without leaking task-specific semantics into the model. We demonstrate superior accuracy over current methods on a range of popular dense task benchmarks, with better computational performance.

title: GhostTac: Manipulating Tactile Sensors without Physical Contact
abstract: Tactile sensors are integral components of modern robotic systems, enabling robots to perceive and interact with the physical environment through tactile feedback. Despite their importance, the physical-layer security of tactile sensors has received little attention in prior work. In this paper, we present GhostTac, to the best of our knowledge, the first contactless attack that manipulates tactile sensing via electromagnetic interference (EMI). We identify that EMI exploits the nonlinear rectification and limited bandwidth amplification effects, allowing carefully crafted EMI signals to be converted into a persistent DC offset that bypasses on-board filtering and induces stable measurement deviations. Building on this mechanism, GhostTac enables fine-grained and controllable manipulation of sensor outputs by reshaping the spatial distribution and manipulating the magnitude at the targeted location. Such interference can induce unintended and harmful robot behaviors, such as causing a domestic robot to exert excessive force, resulting in physical damage or human injury. We evaluate GhostTac on 10 sensor modules and 2 dexterous hands, covering 15 tactile sensors of different types, and demonstrate consistent attack effectiveness across all tested devices. We further present three case studies on tactile grasping, slip detection, and material classification to illustrate practical impacts in real robotic tasks. We envision that our findings shed light on a new physical attack vector against tactile sensing in robotic systems.

title: Multivariate Gaussian process emulation for multifidelity computer models with high-dimensional spatial outputs
abstract: Risk assessment of hurricane-driven storm surge relies on deterministic computer models that produce outputs over a large spatial domain. The surge models can often be run at a range of fidelity levels, with greater precision yielding more accurate simulations. Improved accuracy comes with a significant increase in computational expense, necessitating the development of an emulator which leverages information from the more plentiful low-fidelity outputs to provide fast and accurate predictions of high-fidelity simulations. To properly assess the risk of storm surge over a geographic region, an emulator must account for spatial dependence between outputs yet remain computationally feasible for high-dimensional simulations. To address the challenge of emulating multifidelity computer models with high-dimensional spatial outputs generated at a common set of locations, we exploit the autoregressive cokriging framework to develop two cross-covariance structures to account for spatial dependence. One approach uses a separable covariance structure with a sparse Cholesky prior for the inverse of the cross-covariance matrix; the other involves a low-rank approximation via basis representations. Inferences for these models have been mainly demonstrated in a partial Bayes setting. We demonstrate their predictive performance in the storm surge application and a testbed example.

title: Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents: Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games
abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) uses language models to construct neural network weights without training. We test whether known game mechanics can be compiled into compact agents that generalise to held-out levels, renderings and start states within a game family. Writers receive simulator source with held-out level data removed for 20 privately authored, unpublished ARC-AGI-3-style game families. With a fixed 57k-parameter recurrent architecture, the strongest writer reaches 56% held-out-level success with feedback, while the four main writers' Python players reach 97-100%. An exploratory free-architecture condition reaches 68-90%. Learning from support-level examples transfers much less well, but these learners lack the source information given to writers. Written networks have a program-like structure: 93% of parameters are zero, and 90% of the rest are small integers or powers of two. NumPy players under comparable computation caps reach 91%, versus the networks' 79%. Training the strongest writer's architectures from scratch yields about 1% success within our budget. Written fixed-network weights are fragile, and standard PPO removes most of their success. Prompts for noise robustness increase tolerance by about four orders of magnitude for two of three writers, but PPO makes larger updates and still removes most success. These results demonstrate rule-to-network compilation in this setting, while showing limited benefits over Python programs and no successful combination with the tested PPO fine-tuning.

title: Toward chemically accurate quantum simulations on quantum hardware: A quantum-HPC hybrid approach
abstract: We report one of the most comprehensive experimental demonstrations to date of quantum-computing-based molecular simulation on IQM's Sirius 24-qubit superconducting quantum processor, using up to 16 operational qubits. We employ Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) with the Local Unitary Cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) Ansatz to compute ground-state energies of benchmark molecular systems, including H2, LiH, BeH2, H2O, and NH3. We further introduce the linear-CNOT unitary coupled-cluster singles and doubles Ansatz within the SQD framework, reducing the classical pre-computation overhead at the cost of increased quantum circuit depth and demonstrate its effectiveness by accurately recovering the ground-state energies of H2, LiH, and BeH2. A comparative analysis of the two Ansätze is presented, highlighting their respective merits, demerits, and practical use cases in near-term quantum simulations. In addition, we perform one-dimensional potential energy surface (1D-PES) scans for H2 and HeH+ using STO-3G and 6-31G basis sets and for LiH and BeH2 using STO-3G. We also report the first experimental generation of a full two-dimensional potential energy surface (2D-PES) map, consisting of a 32 × 32 grid in bond length and bond angle, for the water molecule in the STO-3G basis on IQM quantum hardware. Beyond small-molecule benchmarks, we integrate Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) with SQD(LUCJ) to obtain chemically accurate 4-electron-in-4-orbital active-space energies for eight ligand-like molecules, as well as for the pharmacologically relevant amantadine molecular system, representing the first of such experimental demonstrations. Across all studies, the majority of quantum-computed energies agree with reference full configuration interaction results and with DMET-complete active space CI energies for embedded systems, to within chemical accuracy for the chosen basis sets. These results demonstrate the robustness of quantum sampling-based classical diagonalization approaches while highlighting the promise of hybrid embedding strategies combined with near-term Ansätze for advancing quantum chemistry toward classically intractable molecular systems and establishing their practicality on current quantum hardware.

title: Morphological Simplification in Alzheimer's Disease: Computational Analysis and Identification From Connected Speech
abstract: Purpose: Morphology is often regarded as relatively spared in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is rarely modeled in connected speech. This study asked which morphological features distinguish speakers with AD from healthy controls, how well morphology classifies AD compared with other linguistic levels and BERT-based models, and whether the signal exceeds transcript length and vocabulary. Method: Fifty-five automatic measures in eight families, seven of them new and theory-motivated, were computed from participant speech in the ADReSS Cookie Theft descriptions (78 AD, 78 controls) and analyzed with group comparisons, equivalence tests, SHAP, family ablation, likelihood-ratio tests, feature-selection classifiers, and BERT-based models. The automatic measures were validated manually, and models were transferred to two other corpora. Results: Nineteen of 38 measures differed between groups: speakers with AD produced fewer suffixed and inflected words, shorter verbs and nouns, and fewer present-progressive but more past-tense forms (largest effect r = -0.42), whereas errors were rare and statistically equivalent between groups. Eight measures survived adjustment for length and lexical frequency. With test-set feature selection, morphology reached a macro-F1 of 0.85, on par with syntax and above fine-tuned BERT (0.80 over five seeds); fully cross-validated selection gave 0.62. Adding morphology to BERT improved AUC (0.91 vs. 0.89) but not macro-F1. Transfer was limited, although two thirds of the effects kept their direction in mild cognitive impairment. Conclusions: AD connected speech shows morphological simplification and temporal reanchoring rather than breakdown. Morphology is more informative than its reputation suggests. Keywords: Alzheimer's disease; morphology; connected speech; ADReSS; inflection; tense and aspect; SHAP; machine learning; BERT

title: Evaluating AI performance on end-to-end data science projects
abstract: Generative AI is used for knowledge work but many current AI evaluations focus on isolated tasks and constituent parts such as writing code, rather than end-to-end workflows. We test whether AI models can generate end-to-end data science projects. This requires AI models to select a dataset, develop a research question, write code to download, clean, and test data, create figures, and write a reproducible paper. To do this we collect 40 real end-to-end data science projects, then grade them according to a rubric. We use these to build an automated grading pipeline that evaluates data science projects and aligns with the grades that human graders give. For each of nine AI models we then generate five projects and use the automated grader to evaluate them. We find the extent to which generative AI models can complete end-to-end data science projects varies considerably by model. Most recent models did well on structured tasks, but there were considerable differences on tasks that needed judgment such as explaining measurement, writing abstracts, and citing sources. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 averaged 87 per cent and OpenAI’s GPT-5.4 averaged 85 per cent, both around the level of an A for an undergraduate. No model was consistently the best across all aspects of the rubric. These findings suggest that while AI models could soon approximate entry-level data scientists on routine tasks, they require consistent verification and evaluation.

title: Tac-net:triple attention contrastive network for speech complex emotion recognition in real-world scenarios
abstract: Abstract Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) in real-world scenarios remains a challenging task due to uncontrolled acoustic interference and the co-occurrence of complex emotions. Existing single-label approaches often struggle to capture fine-grained emotional semantics while suppressing noise, leading to significant performance degradation in complex environments. To address this, we propose a Triple Attention Contrastive Network (TAC-Net), designed to enhance model robustness through multi-dimensional feature decoupling and reconstruction. First, we introduce a Label-wise Attention Module comprising three collaborative networks: Multi-label Attention (MLA) explicitly models the latent dependencies among emotion tags; Local-Global Attention (LGA) locates key emotional frames temporally while capturing long-range context; and Time-Frequency Attention (TFA) focuses on spectral energy distributions to mitigate channel distortion. Furthermore, a Contrastive Reconstruction-based Fusion Module is incorporated to align heterogeneous features in the latent space via contrastive learning, effectively filtering redundant noise while preserving critical emotional information. Experimental results on the large-scale M³ED and CMU-MOSEI datasets demonstrate that TAC-Net not only significantly outperforms existing unimodal baselines but also achieves competitive performance comparable to multimodal methods in handling multi-label and noisy data.

title: How and When Incivility Unfolds in Online Heatwave Communication: Characterizing Public Discussions on Reddit
abstract: The increasing frequency of heatwaves has sparked widespread concern and emotionally charged, often uncivil, discussions on social media. Drawing on heatwave communication and online incivility research, this study investigates the patterns and antecedents of incivility in Reddit threads from 2023 to 2024 about heatwaves. Specifically, it examines how incivility unfolds across comment threads and how emotional expressions and topics shape uncivil comments. Using natural language processing (i.e., topic modelling and emotion analysis) as well as a large language model-assisted incivility detection approach, we analyzed 1,369 posts, 10,800 firstlayer comments, and 7,297 second-layer comments from eight climate-and country-related subreddits. Results revealed incivility was more prevalent in comments than posts, with firstlayer incivility significantly predicting second-layer instances, hinting at a contagion effect that intensified in deeper threads. Comments expressing anger, disgust, sadness, or surprise were more likely to be uncivil, and controversial topics like climate change attribution, geopolitical conflicts, and regional impacts strongly correlated with higher incivility. Theoretical and practical implications were discussed.

title: Hybridization of Fuzzy Sets and Machine Learning Models for Solving Regression and Classification Problems
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to hybridizing fuzzy sets with machine learning models. The proposed hybrid system is not based on fuzzy rules, so the curse of dimensionality that appears in fuzzy rule-based systems is avoided. The system consists of a fuzzification module and a predictive model realized by a machine learning technique. The fuzzification module transforms each observational variable into fuzzy information described by the fuzzy basis functions. The predictive model uses these fuzzy data as inputs and computes an output using machine learning techniques. In the proposed solution, the fuzzification module can be combined with any predictive model, for example, a neural network, support vector machine, linear discriminant analysis, etc. In tuning the system, a feature selection method is used, which employs fusion of rankings based on a Borda voting system. The results of experiments confirm the efficacy of the presented method and show that the proposed system can improve the results obtained by non-fuzzy systems.

title: Benchmarking hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for power grid optimization problems
abstract: Alternating Current Optimal Power Flow Unit Commitment (AC-OPF-UC) is a difficult mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problem that combines binary generator commitment decisions with nonconvex continuous AC power-flow constraints. In this work, we investigate whether hybrid quantum-classical variational algorithms can improve the solution of single-period AC-OPF-UC relative to classical approaches. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to directly evaluate quantum or hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for single-period AC-OPF-UC with explicit binary commitment variables and the full nonlinear AC power-flow formulation. We consider two candidate algorithms for improving AC-OPF-UC solution quality relative to purely classical methods on ideal quantum hardware. The first applies QAOA directly to a fully discretized formulation of the problem, with equality and inequality constraints incorporated through penalty terms and slack variables. Although conceptually straightforward, this approach requires a prohibitively large number of qubits even for small instances. The second, qubit-efficient approach encodes only the binary generator status variables on a quantum computer, while optimizing the continuous power-flow variables classically for each sampled bitstring. We benchmark this method on randomly generated AC-OPF-UC instances with 5–13 generators and compare it against SCIP, SMAC, and uniform random sampling. Our simulations show that the qubit-efficient hybrid method does not outperform uniform sampling. These results suggest that in order to establish potential advantage of the variational hybrid strategy considered here over the best classical algorithms, if any, much larger system sizes (24+ generators) need to be tested, which is beyond our computational capacity. Alternatively, different approaches, such as quantum versions of branch-and-bound methods, may be more promising.

title: Dual-Score Association-Discrepancy Enhancement for Early-Warning Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection
abstract: Multivariate time-series anomaly detection is important for server monitoring, industrial systems, and intelligent operation and maintenance. Existing point-wise and point-adjusted metrics often fail to show whether an anomalous segment is detected early enough for intervention. This paper proposes a lightweight dual-score enhancement for Anomaly Transformer. The method retains the original multiplicative anomaly score and adds window-normalized reconstruction error and association discrepancy terms, so weak deviations near anomaly onsets become more visible without changing the backbone network or using additional labels. Experiments are conducted on four public multivariate benchmarks, namely, SMD, PSM, SMAP, and MSL, under three random seeds. Compared with the original Anomaly Transformer score, the proposed early-warning union mode improves Raw Event Recall by 0.3435, 0.2408, 0.0995, and 0.0278 on SMD, PSM, SMAP, and MSL, respectively, and reduces mean detection delay by 53.66%, 49.97%, 52.69%, and 39.74%. Event precision, event F1, and false positive rate are also reported in order to make explicit the trade-off between recall and false alarms. Further range- and proximity-aware metrics additionally show that the score-level enhancement improves segment coverage and early warning behavior, while AUPRC remains dataset-dependent. The results indicate that association-discrepancy score enhancement is a practical complement to existing transformer-based anomaly detectors when early warning is more important than point-wise matching alone.
